overview.description: Austrian Dominoes is a unique European variant traditionally played with a Double-Eight set. Its most striking features are the complete removal of all double tiles and a 'brick-layer' tableau formation where tiles are matched side-by-side rather than end-to-end. It is a strategic draw game where players value 'heavier' tiles early in the round.

history.origins: Documented in Vienna as early as 1830, Austrian Dominoes reflects the Central European preference for Double-Eight sets over the more common Double-Six set used in the West.
timeline: 1830: F. Tendler publishes 'Verstand und GlÃ¼ck im Bunde', describing the game with 45 tiles.
1960: Fritz Beck standardizes the 36-tile 'No-Double' variant in 'Domino in vielen Spielarten'.
Present: Remains a traditional past-time in Austrian card clubs and cafes.
history.evolution: The removal of doubles removes the 'spinners' and the high-point anchors typical of Caribbean or American games, shifting focus to pure numerical matching.
history.cultural: Often played in a 'Buki' format (4 players) in rural Austria.

setup.deck: 36 tiles. To prepare, take a Double-Eight set (45 tiles) and discard all 9 doubles (0-0, 1-1... up to 8-8).
setup.dealing: 2 players: 8-9 tiles each. 3 players: 7 tiles each. 4 players: 8 tiles each. Remaining tiles form the 'Stamm' (Boneyard).

rules.objective: To be the first player to reach 100 points across multiple rounds.
rules.gameplay: 1. **Leading**: The player with the heaviest tile (8-7 being the heaviest in this set) leads first. 2. **Matching**: On your turn, you must place a tile where one of its ends matches an available end on the board. 3. **The Draw**: If you cannot play, you must draw from the boneyard until you find a playable tile. (Common house rule: maximum of 3 draws). 4. **Passing**: If the boneyard is empty and you cannot play, you pass. 5. **Ending**: A round ends when one player 'Dominoes' (empties their hand) or when the game is blocked.
keyRules: No Doubles: The absence of doubles means every tile is distinct and has two different numbers.
The 8-7 Lead: The highest tile in play (8-7) always starts the first hand.
Brick Formation: The tableau grows in two directions from the starting tile, but specifically in a side-by-side matching manner.

strategy.basic: Keep a variety of numbers in your hand. Since there are no doubles, you don't have to worry about 'blocking' your own suits in the same way.
strategy.intermediate: High-Pip Management: Early in the game, try to play your 8s and 7s. If someone else dominoes, you don't want to be caught with high-counting tiles in your hand.
strategy.advanced: Boneyard Counting: Since there are only 36 tiles and you know exactly which ones are missing (the doubles), you can more accurately track which tiles are left in the boneyard vs in opponents' hands.
tips: If you are playing the 4-player block variant, remember that there is no boneyard. Information is perfect if you can track all 36 tiles.
The 'Brick' layout can sometimes be confusing; visualize the ends as 'slots' that must match.

list.name: Buki
list.description: A 4-player block version where all titles are dealt out and no drawing is allowed.
list.emptyOverridesReason: Buki is a related gambling-style variant; stake handling and detailed payments are not yet modeled as engine overrides in this file.

difficulty.easy: Does not understand the brick layout; often misses legal moves. Draws from the boneyard even when it has a playable tile.
difficulty.medium: Prioritizes playing tiles with high pip counts. Understands the 100-point goal and plays defensively when an opponent is at 90+.
difficulty.hard: Perfectly tracks all 36 tiles. Calculates the exact number of 8s remaining in circulation and uses this to block opponents.

considerations: AI must maintain a 'Removed Tiles' bitmask including all doubles (0-0 through 8-8).
The brick matching logic is a custom adjacency check.

additional: Fritz Beck - Domino in vielen Spielarten (Vienna, 1960)

ante.reason: Austrian Dominoes is a draw-and-match game with no betting or ante.

deal.reason: Dealing is done via custom deal_tiles action; no generic deal action.

reveal_market.reason: No market pile; tiles are in talon (boneyard) and hands only.

buy_market.reason: There is no market or purchase mechanic in this domino game.

buy_stock.reason: Players draw from talon when blocked; no buy-from-stock action.

fold.reason: Players pass only when boneyard is empty and they cannot play.

check.reason: No betting rounds; check does not apply to Austrian Dominoes.

call.reason: No betting; call is not used in this domino game.

bet.reason: Scoring is by opponent pips per round; no wagering.

raise.reason: No betting; raise does not apply to this game.

declare.reason: No declaration phase; players match tiles to the brick layout.

reveal_hand.reason: Hands stay private until play; no reveal-hand phase.

award_pot.reason: Points are tallied via count_opposing_pips; no pot to award.

play_card.reason: Tile play uses custom match_tile_brick action for brick layout.

draw.reason: Drawing from boneyard is via custom draw_from_talon action.

discard.reason: Tiles are played to the tableau only; no discard pile in this game.

pass.reason: Pass occurs only when blocked and boneyard empty; no explicit pass action.

bid.reason: No bidding; heaviest tile leads; play is match-only.

meld.reason: No melding; tiles are matched side-by-side on the brick tableau.

go_out.reason: Round ends when a player dominoes or game is blocked; no go_out action.

engine.handRankingSystem: There is no separate poker-style hand ranking; tiles are compared by pip totals when evaluating blocked hands or choosing the initial leader.
engine.deckDescription: Austrian Dominoes uses a double-eight domino set adapted to 36 tiles. The original set has 45 tiles covering every combination from 0-0 up to 8-8; for this game all nine doubles are removed so every tile shows two different pip values.
engine.suitDescription: Tiles are not grouped into suits. Each end shows a pip value from zero to eight, and tiles may be played whenever one end matches the value showing on an open end of the brick-style tableau.
engine.rankDescription: There is no fixed rank hierarchy like playing cards. Tiles are compared by their total pip count only when selecting the initial leader or resolving a blocked game; normally the holder of the heaviest tile, such as the 8-7, leads the first round.

hero.title: AUSTRIAN DOMINO
hero.subtitle: The Bricklayers' Challenge
hero.tagline: No doubles. No safety. Build your way to the 100-point peak.

synthesis.shortDescription: Discover the traditional domino game of Central Europe. With the nine doubles removed, strategies shift and the unique side-matching bricks create a beautiful, tactical tableau. Master the 36-tile set and lead with your heaviest pips.

prompts.human: Welcome to Austrian Dominoes! We've removed all nine doubles, so you have 36 tiles in play. The 8-7 is the highest card out there. Match your tiles to the sides of the bricks and see if you can reach 100 points first!
prompts.ai: Game: Austrian Dominoes. Type: Match-and-Draw. Rules: Double-8 set, 9 doubles removed (36 total). Matching: Side-to-side brick style. Goal: 100 points (opponents' pips).

scoring.winCondition: First player to 100 points wins the game.
scoring.splitRules: In case of a tie in a blocked game, the player with the lowest pip total wins. If pips are equal, the round is a draw.

nullReasons.cardValues: Individual tiles do not carry fixed point values; scoring is based on the total pip count of tiles left in a player’s hand.
